title: The winner that ate the portfolio
intro: A doubling gold rally has turned your 8% insurance sleeve into 17% of the portfolio. Steer — and watch the allocation-discipline meter.

nodes.text: Gold has doubled. The 5–10% you bought as insurance is now 15–20% — 'a bet that nobody actually decided to make.' What do you do?

choices.label: Let the winner run — momentum is momentum
choices.note: You now hold a concentrated bet you never chose.

choices.label: Rebalance: sell enough to return to the allocation you set
choices.note: The adviser's version — trim what doubled.

choices.label: Keep the holding, but cut the gold SIP so new money stops feeding the drift

nodes.text: Six months on, gold corrects 18%. The 'winner' gave back more than the rest of the portfolio earned. The drift was a risk decision made by inattention. Recover?

choices.label: Rebalance now and write the rule down for next time

nodes.text: You sell back to 8%. Capital-gains tax is due on the trimmed slice, and gold keeps rising for two more months — the neighbours gloat. Then it corrects. How do you frame the episode?

choices.label: Rebalancing means sometimes selling what keeps rising — that's the price of the discipline
choices.note: The point exactly: you can't collect insurance and momentum at once.

choices.label: Regret the sale — next time hold until the exact top
choices.note: Top-timing is the fantasy that causes the drift in the first place.

nodes.text: You cut the gold SIP from ₹25k to ₹7k. The allocation drifts back only slowly — but no tax, no timing call. Months later gold is still 14% of the book. Enough?

choices.label: Pair the SIP cut with a partial sell-back toward target
choices.note: Flow fixes the future; only selling fixes the present.

choices.label: Leave it — the SIP cut alone will get there eventually
choices.note: Meanwhile you carry double the intended gold risk through whatever comes.

nodes.text: Last question: what should trigger the next rebalance?

choices.label: A written rule — annual date or a ±5% band breach, whichever first
Whenever the news makes the allocation feel wrong

ending.principle: Insurance that doubles is no longer insurance — rebalancing by rule returns the portfolio to the risk you actually chose.
ending.debrief: The issue's line carries the whole lesson: the drifted allocation is 'a bet nobody actually decided to make.' Both cures work — the sell-back (fast, taxed) and the SIP cut (slow, tax-free) — and pair well. What makes either stick is the written trigger: a date or a band, so the next rally rebalances the portfolio in the right direction.

ending.principle: Feelings rebalance portfolios in the wrong direction; rules rebalance them in the right one.
ending.debrief: Every step that lost meter points shared one shape: letting attention, momentum or regret make the allocation decision. The mechanics are easy — trim the winner, cut its SIP. The discipline is the written rule that fires without asking how you feel.
